name: Scientific Evidence and Data
what: This subtopic covers how to collect, record and represent data appropriately. It includes the distinction between qualitative and quantitative data, the concept of resolution, how to construct correct results tables and graphs, and how to identify trends in data.
why: Correctly organising and representing data is a core scientific skill assessed in VCE. Well-structured tables and graphs make it possible to identify patterns, support or refute hypotheses, and communicate findings clearly.

items.title: I can distinguish between qualitative and quantitative data
items.what: Qualitative data is descriptive and expressed in words rather than numbers, such as colour, appearance or texture. Quantitative data is numerical, based on counting or measuring, and is expressed with appropriate units.
items.why: The type of data collected determines how it should be recorded and represented graphically. Misidentifying data type leads to incorrect graph choice and lost marks in VCE assessment tasks.
items.example: In the invertase experiment, observing that the glucose test strip 'turned dark brown' is qualitative data. Recording that the glucose concentration was 10.0 mg mL^-1 is quantitative data.

items.title: I can explain what resolution means and how it affects data recording
items.what: Resolution refers to the smallest change in a quantity that results in a noticeable change in the reading on a measuring instrument. The resolution of the instrument determines how many decimal places can be recorded.
items.why: Recording data to more decimal places than the instrument allows is scientifically dishonest and inaccurate. Recording to fewer decimal places than possible wastes the precision available from the instrument.
items.example: A gas syringe with markings every 1 mL has a resolution of 1.0 mL, allowing estimation to the nearest 0.1 mL (e.g. 11.3 mL). A burette with markings every 0.1 mL has a resolution of 0.1 mL, allowing estimation to 0.01 mL (e.g. 40.73 mL).

items.title: I can construct a correctly formatted results table
items.what: A results table must include a title referencing both variables, column headings with units, the independent variable in the first column, consistent decimal places across all values, results for all trials, and a calculated mean that excludes outliers.
items.why: An incorrectly formatted table is a common source of lost marks in VCE. Each convention — from decimal consistency to the placement of units in headings — reflects professional scientific recording practice.
items.example: Column heading 'Concentration of glucose (mg mL^-1)' is correct. Writing '10.0 mg mL^-1' inside a cell is incorrect — units belong in the heading only. All values in a column should be recorded to the same number of decimal places, e.g. 0.00, 1.00, 3.00, not 0, 1, 3.

items.title: I can choose the correct graph type to represent a given dataset
items.what: Continuous data (measured quantities such as time, temperature, concentration or volume) should be represented as a line graph with a line of best fit. Discrete data (countable, distinct categories) should be represented as a bar graph with gaps between bars.
items.why: Using a bar graph for continuous data, or a line graph for discrete data, is incorrect and reflects a misunderstanding of data types. VCE marking rubrics specifically assess correct graph type selection.
items.example: In the invertase experiment, glucose concentration measured over time (0 s, 60 s, 120 s, 180 s, 240 s, 300 s) is continuous data — a line graph is appropriate. If comparing the number of reactions that produced a precipitate across four different metal types, a bar graph would be appropriate.

items.title: I can construct a correctly labelled graph with a line of best fit
items.what: A graph must include a title, fully labelled axes with units, the independent variable on the x-axis, the dependent variable on the y-axis, evenly spaced axis scales, and a line of best fit that is drawn so the distances of points above and below the line are approximately equal.
items.why: A line of best fit shows the general trend and is used for making predictions. Common errors — such as connecting the dots rather than drawing a smooth trend line, or not starting scales at appropriate values — reduce the quality and interpretability of a graph.
items.example: In the invertase experiment, the x-axis is labelled 'Time (s)' with values 0, 60, 120, 180, 240, 300, and the y-axis is 'Concentration of glucose produced (mg mL^-1)' with values 0 to 25. The line of best fit is smooth and does not need to pass through the first or last point.

items.title: I can identify and describe trends in experimental data
items.what: Identifying trends means describing the overall relationship between the independent and dependent variables, noting any changes in the gradient, and quoting specific data values from tables or graphs to support the description.
items.why: Trend identification is the basis of discussion and conclusion writing. Unsupported trend statements ('the results increased') without reference to data are insufficient for VCE extended response tasks.
items.example: In the invertase experiment: 'The concentration of glucose increased from 0.00 mg mL^-1 at 0 s to 20.0 mg mL^-1 at 180 s in the presence of invertase, after which it plateaued and remained constant at 20.0 mg mL^-1 through to 300 s.'
